column4: The contrast between one who crawls face-down and one who “walks evenly on a straight path” makes the traveller’s manner determine how the same journey is made.
The rider literally settles on the animal’s back in لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِ, the exact riding sense the section uncovers inside سوّى.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى repeats the section’s promise almost word for word and turns moral disposition into a direction made easy to travel.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَى uses the same causative “make easy” for the opposite destination, proving that compliance alone does not determine where the mount goes.
إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَى makes God the one responsible for showing the route, matching the section’s guide who goes ahead.
لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى joins “the most wretched” directly to entering fire, the same sequence as 87:11-12.
وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا الْأَتْقَى reverses 87:11: the worst person keeps the reminder aside, while the most God-fearing is himself kept aside from the fire.
“He gave each thing its created form, then guided” restages 87:2-3 as a single answer: fitting a creature and directing it belong together.
Whoever follows God’s guidance “will neither stray nor suffer”; following the leader prevents both loss of route and the شقاء opposed to ease.
God makes the earth ذَلُولًا, docile, and tells people to walk on its shoulders; the road itself becomes the compliant mount imagined by the section.
Abraham says “follow me; I will guide you to an even path,” explicitly staging a guide in front, a follower, and صِرَاطًا سَوِيًّا.
صِرَاطِ السَّوِيِّ and وَمَنِ اهْتَدَى bring the section’s “middle/even place” and guidance roots together in one question about whose route proves right.
“Seize him and drag him to the middle of Hell” combines a captive being led, physical motion, and سَوَاءِ الْجَحِيمِ, the section’s wrong endpoint.
فَاهْدُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيمِ uses “guide” for prisoners driven to Hell’s road, a deliberate reversal of guidance toward the easy good.
Guidance opens the chest, while misguidance makes it tight “as though climbing into the sky”; moral direction is felt as easy passage versus punishing ascent.
The one who turns from his Lord’s reminder is made to enter عَذَابًا صَعَدًا, an arduous rising punishment that joins avoidance to the difficult climb.
The rejecter of God’s signs is burdened with صَعُودًا, a punishing ascent, giving the section’s mountain ridge its adverse moral route.
فَمَا اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الْهَدْيِ combines what is readily available from يسر with الهدي as sacrificial livestock, making the two root families meet in an actual led animal.
إِذِ انْبَعَثَ أَشْقَاهَا places the same superlative “most wretched” in motion in the story of a she-camel, joining the traveller word to a mishandled animal.
God’s messenger identifies “God’s she-camel and her drink”; this is the divine animal beside the moving أَشْقَاهَا of the preceding ayah.
The people deny the messenger and hamstring the camel, showing where the route of the moving “most wretched” ends.
فَمَا لَهُمْ عَنِ التَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ asks why they turn aside from the reminder, the same action the section reads in يَتَجَنَّبُهَا.
Their avoidance of the reminder becomes a herd scene: they are “like startled wild asses,” turning spiritual refusal into animal flight.
The wild asses flee from a lion, completing the preceding ayah’s concrete image of the reminder-avoider rushing away rather than walking calmly.
God creates pairs and provides ships and livestock “which you ride,” supplying the vehicles on whose backs the next ayah’s settling occurs.
After mounting, the riders confess that they are returning to their Lord; the compliant vehicle becomes an image of the journey’s final direction.
A dependent man is a burden wherever his master directs him, while the other commands justice “and is on a straight path”; ability and manner divide travellers.
ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ says God then made the human being’s path easy, explicitly joining the road to the section’s causative ease.
إِنَّا هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ presents one shown road followed in two moral manners, gratitude or ingratitude.
وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ shows two elevated roads and makes guidance itself a view of the two ridges.
فَلَا اقْتَحَمَ الْعَقَبَةَ says the traveller did not undertake the steep pass, the direct adverse counterpart to the easier ridge in the dictionary image.
Adam is warned that leaving the garden will make him تَشْقَى, locating hardship at the far end of a wrong departure.
The Qur’an was not sent to the Prophet لِتَشْقَى, so revelation and his commission are expressly bounded away from the section’s hardship root.
Moses asks وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي, the same root as the promise to make the Prophet fit for the easiest course.
Abraham asks وَاجْنُبْنِي وَبَنِيَّ to be kept away from idols; the same root works rightly by removing the worshipper from the false object.
The saved speaker looks down and sees his former companion فِي سَوَاءِ الْجَحِيمِ, at the exact “middle of Hell” named by the section.
God owns the path’s intended direction, while “some of it deviates”; guidance and the road’s lateral departure are held in one image.
The command to turn from one who turned from God’s reminder and wanted only worldly life joins 87’s avoided reminder to its preference for the nearer life.
Turning away from God’s reminder produces a constricted life immediately after the promise that following guidance prevents straying and wretchedness.
The revelation makes those who fear tremble, then soften to God’s remembrance, and is called God’s guidance; fear, reminder, and guidance converge.
Livestock carry burdens to a land people could reach only بِشِقِّ الْأَنْفُسِ; the mount converts bodily hardship into attainable travel.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created لِتَرْكَبُوهَا, supplying the literal riding animals beneath the section’s easy-guided mount.
Pilgrims arrive on foot and “on every lean camel” from every deep mountain road, joining gait, mount, and long pass.
God subdues livestock for people, “and some of them they ride”; the subjected animal is the section’s readily guided beast made concrete.
God makes livestock so that people may ride some and eat some, an explicit statement of the mount’s provision.
Livestock bear travellers just as ships do, expanding the previous ayah’s ride into the shared function of vehicles.
People are carried “on them and on ships,” placing animal mount and vessel under one travel image.
The ayah repeatedly permits what is easy of recitation while naming travellers walking through the land, bringing ease, gait, and revelation together.
God wants to lighten the human being because humanity was created weak; lightness answers precisely to the section’s weak supported walker and light legs.
God lightens the believers’ duty because He knows weakness is among them, again pairing ضعف with divinely granted lightness.
Moses asks God to strengthen his back through Aaron, a concrete human counterpart to the weak person who moves by leaning on companions.
Moses asks that Aaron share his task, turning support into companionship along the commissioned journey.
Moses asks that Aaron be sent with him رِدْءًا, as supporting reinforcement, closely matching the secondary image of a weak person relying on another.
God promises “We will strengthen your arm through your brother,” answering Moses’ weakness with a companion’s support.
The servants of the Merciful “walk on the earth gently,” the closest Qur’anic staging of the section’s calm, unhurried, good gait.
وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ commands moderation in one’s walk, defining the deliberate pace opposed to panicked flight.
The ban on strutting adds that the walker can neither split the earth nor reach the mountains in height, opposing calm gait while joining walking to ascent.
“Do not walk exultantly on earth” supplies the rejected gait whose correction follows in 31:19.
يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ الْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ الْعُسْر states the divine preference for ease over hardship in the same paired vocabulary.
The Qur’an is made easy on the Prophet’s tongue so he may give good news and warn, joining prophetic readiness to effective reminder.
The revelation is made easy in the Prophet’s tongue “so that they may remember,” explicitly linking ease to the reminder’s reception.
“We made the Qur’an easy for remembrance” directly connects the section’s ease with the act some hearers accept and others avoid.
The repeated promise that the Qur’an was made easy for remembrance shows that this ease remains available after a people’s refusal.
A third repetition makes the ease of remembrance the stable road offered across changing warning narratives.
The fourth repetition confirms that the object made easy is consistently the reminder itself.
Whoever fears God is granted يُسْرًا in his affair, linking the fearing hearer of 87:10 to the ease promised in 87:8.
سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا presents hardship and ease as successive conditions under God’s making.
فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا places ease alongside hardship rather than merely after it, clarifying the section’s shared road with differing experience.
The immediate repetition insists again that ease accompanies the difficult stretch.
فَسَنَقُولُ لَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْرًا is another future promise of ease in a person’s appointed affair, close in stance to 87:8.
God says He placed no constriction in the religion, defining the revealed course as one fitted against disabling hardship.
The Day is عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ, explicitly “not easy” for rejecters and thus the eschatological boundary of the promised easy course.
The Qur’an guides to “that which is most upright,” making the reminder itself the guide walking ahead on the best-aligned course.
Revelation is a light by which God guides, and the Prophet guides to a straight path; divine and prophetic leading are distinguished within one route.
The jinn describe the post-Mosaic book as guiding to truth and to a straight path, recognizing revelation as a road guide.
فَذَكِّرْ بِالْقُرْآنِ مَنْ يَخَافُ وَعِيدِ addresses the same Prophet and joins reminder specifically to the hearer who fears.
The warning reaches the one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, pairing following with the receptive fearer.
The Prophet is a warner specifically for the one who fears the Hour, matching the stance that the fearing person will remember.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنْتَ مُذَكِّرٌ repeats the command and defines the Prophet’s role as reminder.
وَذَكِّرْ فَإِنَّ الذِّكْرَى تَنْفَعُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ directly states when reminder benefits, the condition posed in 87:9.
Whenever a renewed reminder comes from the Merciful, its hearers turn away from it, restaging the deliberate bypass of 87:11.
The ayah asks whether the one who guides to truth deserves to be followed over one who cannot proceed unless guided, exposing leader and dependent follower.
The believing man says “follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct,” explicitly assuming the section’s forward guide position.
As Moses physically turns toward Midian, he hopes his Lord will guide him to the level road, making guidance literal route-finding.
At the blocked sea during flight, Moses says “my Lord is with me; He will guide me,” so guidance arrives inside an urgent physical journey.
Moses asks to follow the knowledgeable servant so that he may teach him right guidance, staging learner behind guide on a shared journey.
The Prophet calls “this is my way” and names himself and those who follow him, giving the mission a leader-and-followers road form.
The command “follow him so that you may be guided” makes following the Messenger the human motion corresponding to divine guidance.
A man comes running from the farthest end of the city and commands “follow the messengers,” joining bodily motion to choosing leaders.
“Follow those who ask no payment and are guided” identifies why the running man’s proposed leaders are fit to follow.
“Guide us to the straight path” is the direct prayer to be shown and led along the right road.
At the descent from the garden, following God’s guidance secures the travellers from fear and grief, paralleling the later Adamic promise in 20:123.
God’s straight path is to be followed, while following the other roads disperses travellers away from it; the journey forks by obedience.
The arrogant see the path of right guidance and refuse it, but see the path of error and take it, making the wrong route a deliberate preference.
Each person acts according to his own manner, while God knows who is “more guided in way”; this closely states that the road differs through its walker.
Those who listen and follow the best of what is said are precisely those God has guided, making ready following the mark of guidance.
Hearers who fail to understand are likened to livestock and called still farther astray from the path, the failed human opposite of a rightly led animal.
God makes the earth a bed and puts roads in it “so that you may be guided,” joining prepared terrain to finding direction.
God spreads the earth as a cradle and threads roads through it for people, the physical counterpart to His giving each creature form and guidance in 20:50.
Firm mountains contain broad passes “so that they may be guided,” making guidance movement through mountain openings.
Mountains stabilize the earth and rivers and roads are provided “so that you may be guided,” placing guidance in a traversable landscape.
Landmarks and stars supply the traveller’s means of guidance, completing the preceding ayah’s roads.
The spread earth lets people travel through its spacious mountain ways, a direct landscape for the section’s light-moving traveller.
God guides people through the darknesses of land and sea, presenting guidance as practical navigation.
The stars are made so people may find guidance through darkness on land and sea, identifying created signs that go before the traveller.
A near gain and moderate journey would have drawn followers, but the actual distance seemed hard; ease and hardship expose the quality of following.
Disbelievers are driven in companies to Hell, a collective journey whose destination matches the wrong road’s fire.
Those who feared God are driven in companies to the Garden, forming the opposite procession on the other destination.
The God-fearing are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, giving their final journey a dignified manner of arrival.
The criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, opposing the preceding delegation in both manner and destination.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are called worst in place and farther astray from the path, the inverted gait and route of 67:22.
The ayah contrasts God’s guidance with loss of guides, then gathers the lost on their faces toward Hell, turning misguidance into a bodily procession.
Those who are شَقُوا are in the Fire, another direct bond between wretchedness and the fiery endpoint.
The people in the Fire confess that their شِقْوَتُنَا overcame them and that they were astray, joining hardship to loss of route.
Abraham withdraws from the idols his people invoke and hopes not to be شَقِيًّا in prayer, joining right separation from idols to escape from wretchedness.
Jesus says God did not make him overbearing and شَقِيًّا, a character-level negation of the wretched figure who turns aside from reminder.
Those who اجْتَنَبُوا الطَّاغُوتَ and turn toward God use avoidance in the saving direction, opposite the person who avoids the reminder.
Every messenger commands worship of God and avoidance of false powers; the ayah then distinguishes those guided from those fixed in error.
The command to avoid the pollution of idols gives the same avoidance action the right object, unlike keeping divine reminder at one’s side.
Rejecting false power and holding the firm handhold combines right avoidance with secure support, reversing both the object avoided and the unsupported traveller.
When favored, the human “turns away and withdraws to his side” in أَعْرَضَ وَنَأَى بِجَانِبِهِ, bodily staging the section’s bypassing refusal.
The same phrase أَعْرَضَ وَنَأَى بِجَانِبِهِ pictures the recipient of favor turning away to his side, rather than continuing behind the guide.
The sun veers to the cave’s right and passes its left while the ayah closes with God’s guidance, bringing lateral avoidance and true guidance into one scene.
الَّذِي خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ repeats creation followed by proportioning and balance, the ordinary sense from which the saddle image grows.
فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّى repeats the compact sequence “created, then proportioned,” directly echoing 87:2.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it uses سَوَّاهَا immediately before the two moral inclinations are disclosed.
The soul is inspired with both its rebellion and its God-consciousness, supplying the two directions opened by its proportioning.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the soul, the right handling of the fitted traveller before the camel story begins.
Failure belongs to the one who buries the soul, the opposing direction that leads into the action of أَشْقَاهَا.
رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّاهَا joins height and proportioning in one act, matching the section’s observation that settling/rising language sits inside سوّى.
The ark “settled on al-Judi” in وَاسْتَوَتْ عَلَى الْجُودِيِّ, extending the rider’s settling sense from an animal to a vessel after travel.
Noah is told what to say once he and his companions have settled on the ship, another vehicle use of اسْتَوَيْتَ.
مَكَانًا سُوًى names an equally accessible middle meeting place, exactly the spatial sense cited in the section.
Abraham says “I am going to my Lord; He will guide me,” making his separation and divine guidance a first-person journey.
The panting chargers stage speed and exertion at the opposite pole from the dictionary’s calm, unhurried gait; the link is a deliberate contrast of animal movement.
Moses asks for a minister from his family, initiating the companion-support scene that becomes explicit in 20:31.
Naming Aaron as the requested minister identifies the person on whom Moses’ back and mission will rely.
The woman approaches Moses “walking with modesty”; this is a particular composed gait, though the ayah does not connect it explicitly to guidance.
The sacrificial camels fall عَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهَا, onto their sides; this animal scene preserves the concrete “side” beneath the section’s جنب word-family.
The well-bred standing steeds foreground a horse’s controlled posture, a plausible Qur’anic counterpart to the easy-guided horse in the dictionary branch.
The scene focuses on the horses’ legs and necks, details that meet the section’s light legs, though the ayah’s disputed action does not itself assert ease.
The cave youths ask God to “prepare for us from our affair right conduct”; preparing a fit course parallels the dictionary sense of ease as readiness.
God will “prepare for you facility in your affair,” a nonlexical parallel to being made ready for the easier course.
The trumpet’s day is called a difficult day, setting up the next ayah’s explicit denial that it will be easy for rejecters.
The Prophet is not a controller over the hearers; this bounds his reminding role, while their decision to follow or turn aside remains theirs.
Human beings are carried on land and sea, a broad vehicle image that supports the section’s traveller without specifying a mount’s docility.
The Day divides people into شَقِيّ and سَعِيد; the next ayah supplies the wretched group’s fiery destination.
Moses’ sister watches him عَنْ جُنُبٍ, from the side and unnoticed; this preserves the lateral sense behind leading or keeping something alongside.
God proportions the human being and gives faculties, another creation use of سوّى that shows fitness before directed human action.
The invitation to look at how camels were created activates the section’s camel-hump coverings and mount, though riding is not stated here.
The adjacent invitation to look at mountains activates the long mountain ridge placed beside the camel image in the section.
The spread earth supplies the surface across which the preceding camel and mountain images can become a journey, but no guide is named.
الْهَدْيَ مَعْكُوفًا أَنْ يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ is sacrificial livestock prevented from reaching its destination; this different هدي sense gives a led animal a blocked road.
هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ uses هدي for an offering that reaches the Kaaba, a different root sense whose animal is assigned a destination.
The question “What will make you know what the steep pass is?” announces that the physical ascent will be interpreted by the following deeds.
Freeing a bound neck is the first act identified with crossing the steep pass, turning ascent into costly release.
Feeding during famine is the next content of the difficult ascent, showing what effort on the right road consists of.
The related orphan identifies one recipient of the feeding that constitutes the pass.
The destitute person in dust identifies the other recipient and keeps the elevated road tied to aiding the lowly.
Faith and mutual counsel to patience and mercy complete the interpretation of those who successfully take the steep road.
If a debtor is weak or unable to dictate, his guardian speaks justly for him; it is a precise legal scene of a weak person proceeding through another’s support.
The oppressed men, women, and children ask for a protecting ally and helper; this parallels dependence on companions, though no walking scene is present.
Giving and fearing God are the traveller’s dispositions that make the promise of the easy course in 92:7 intelligible.
Affirming the best supplies the immediate response to revelation for which the person is made ready for ease in 92:7.
Miserliness and imagined self-sufficiency begin the opposite route whose destination is hardship in 92:10.
Denying the best identifies refusal of the reminder as the rider’s choice before he is made ready for the arduous course.
The denier’s wealth cannot help “when he falls,” giving the hard route of 92:10 a bodily downward outcome.
The warning of a blazing fire supplies the destination approached by “the most wretched” in the next ayah.
The most wretched is defined as the one who denied and turned away, exactly explaining the behaviour pictured as passing the reminder by.
Those who complete the steep pass are named companions of the right, giving the successfully climbed road its community and destination.
Those who reject the signs are companions of the left, the opposing company reached by refusing the pass.
A closed-over fire is the endpoint of the left-hand company, completing the passage’s two-road contrast.
Thamud’s collective denial sets the scene for the movement of “its most wretched” and shows that his attack embodies a people’s rejected warning.
Whoever exchanges faith for unbelief “has strayed from the middle of the road,” directly joining سوء choice to سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ.
After covenant obligations and a promise of support, disbelief is said to stray from سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ, the road’s balanced middle.
People who follow earlier desires are said to have gone astray from سَوَاءِ السَّبِيلِ, making the middle road something inherited error can leave.
Taking God’s enemies as confidants after truth arrived is again called straying from سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ, a relational act expressed as departure from the road’s middle.
Believers are commanded فَاجْتَنِبُوهُ concerning intoxicants, gambling, cult stones, and divining arrows; avoidance receives the right harmful object rather than the reminder.
Satan uses intoxicants and gambling to bar people from God’s remembrance and prayer, explaining why the preceding ayah commands avoiding them instead of being diverted from reminder.
الْحَوَايَا means entrails here, not a saddle cloth, yet its enclosing root occurs beside what animals’ backs bear and so illuminates the haviyye word-family cautiously.
Noah commands his people to board the ark in God’s name, marking the beginning and course of the vehicle journey that ends when it settles in 11:44.
God’s making livestock for human possession supplies the animals that the next ayah describes as subdued and ridden.
The same ayah names livestock made for carrying loads and forbids following Satan’s footsteps, bringing the pack animal and the choice of whom to follow together.
Livestock provide beauty when driven home and sent out, a controlled herd movement related to the animal led calmly beside its keeper.
God creates creatures that move on bellies, two legs, or four, showing created fitting and guidance through distinct forms of locomotion.
Those who fear God and believe His messenger receive a light by which they walk, turning receptive fear and following into enabled movement.
Those who support God are promised divine support and firm feet, a precise bodily answer to the section’s weak, wavering walker.
A foot can slip after being firm because one barred others from God’s path; wrong allegiance becomes loss of footing on the road.
God gives Moses the Book and appoints Aaron with him as a minister, repeating the companion support that answers Moses’ need for strength.
God removes the Prophet’s burden, supplying the relief that precedes the repeated promise of ease in the same surah.
The removed load had weighed down the Prophet’s back, a bodily burden that closely complements the supported back and light gait in the section.
The truly helpless are those without a means and unable to find a way, joining human weakness to the practical inability to be guided onto a route.
God does not let a people stray after guiding them until He clarifies what they must guard against, holding guidance and right avoidance in one rule.
The listened-to Qur’an is said to guide to right conduct, so the reminder itself becomes the guide that receptive hearers follow.
People in the Fire confess that they obeyed leaders and great men who misled them from the path, exposing the ruin caused by following false guides.
The wrongdoer wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger, expressing missed discipleship as failure to travel behind the right leader.
The reminder is for whoever wills “to go straight,” presenting reception of revelation as the traveller’s desire for an upright course.
Human willingness to go straight remains under God’s will, marking the boundary between the rider’s response and the One who makes the course possible.
Wrongdoers sit on every path threatening people and barring believers from God’s way, turning the roadside itself into an obstacle to guidance.
The disputant twists his side in order to mislead others from God’s path, joining bodily side-turning to active diversion from the road.
The donkey carrying books pictures a burden-bearing animal whose rider-like load produces no response to revelation, a warning against mere carriage of reminder.
God carries human progeny in the laden ship, another vehicle provided to bear travellers who cannot bear themselves.
God creates counterparts to the ship “which they ride,” explicitly extending the vehicle image beyond the laden vessel.
God subjects ships to run through the sea by His command, giving the vehicle the compliant following that the section assigns to the easy-guided mount.
Travellers enjoy a ship’s good wind and then face a storm, staging ease and distress as two experiences on the same vehicle and route.
Those who ask the Prophet for mounts but find nothing to carry them turn away in tears, making lack of a vehicle the concrete limit on willing followers.
Pharaoh goes ahead of his people on the Day of Judgment and brings them to the Fire, the exact inverse of a guide preceding followers toward safety.
Pharaoh and his chiefs are made leaders who invite to the Fire, a formal reversal of leaders who guide by God’s command.
The wrongdoers, their kinds, and their objects of worship are gathered into the captive procession that the next ayah guides to Hell’s road.
The procession is stopped for questioning after being led toward Hell, distinguishing this ayah’s halt from 37:23’s direction of travel.
With shackles and chains around their necks, the condemned are dragged, closely realizing the dictionary’s secondary scene of leading a captive alongside.
The dragged captives are taken through boiling water and into fire, supplying the destination of the movement in 40:71.
The rejecters found their fathers astray, identifying the false predecessors whose tracks they hurry along in the next ayah.
They rush headlong upon their fathers’ traces, combining wrong following with a hurried gait opposed to the section’s calm, well-guided walk.
Moses is commanded to take God’s servants by night and strike a dry road through the sea, a guide leading followers on a divinely prepared path without fear.
Pharaoh follows the guided party with his forces and is overwhelmed by the sea, showing the disastrous pursuer on the same opened route.
The passage concludes that Pharaoh misled his people and did not guide them, explicitly judging the false leader’s direction.
The bee is told to eat from fruits and travel its Lord’s paths ذُلُلًا, joining an animal, divinely given routes, and docile ease in one formulation.
Abraham’s line are made leaders who guide by God’s command, stating the forward human leadership implicit in the section’s definition of هادي.
Leaders are appointed from among the Israelites to guide by God’s command when they show patience, tying guidance to qualified endurance on the course.
A debtor in hardship is granted delay until مَيْسَرَةٍ, presenting ease as a reachable condition that answers present constriction.
Those made happy are in the Garden with an unbroken gift, the destination opposite the fire of the شَقُوا in 11:106.
Their sides leave their beds as they call on God in fear and hope; bodily “sides” enact a saving separation directed toward worship.
God promises the Prophet forgiveness, completed favor, and guidance on a straight path, paralleling the personal promise of being made ready for ease.
The Prophet declares that his Lord guided him to a straight path, the upright religion of Abraham, joining prophetic route and the named patriarch.
God chooses Abraham and guides him to a straight path, making the figure named at surah 87’s close a traveller under divine guidance.
God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining invitation, road, and destination.
